"The provided sentences discuss the historical notion of 'great men' who are believed to have the power to direct and change the course of history through their exceptional talents, courage, and charisma. This idea, originating in the 19th century, has persisted despite the rise of egalitarian and Marxist social theories, as well as the advent of 'history from below' championed by EP Thompson in the 1960s.

The article highlights the Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle, who viewed figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad as standout heroes who fundamentally and permanently changed the world around them. Carlyle believed that the mass of humanity could merely watch, marvel, and tamely follow these top-down 'makers and shakers of universal history.' This notion is described as a 'daft idea,' yet it remains seductive and long-lived.

The article suggests that in the modern era, such 'great' men are typically not heroes, as the word is commonly understood, but rather anti-heroes or, more precisely, villains. These individuals still wield significant power and believe they have a special mission or calling to lead and act as saviors of peoples and nations. They are characterized as ruthless and arrogant enough to impose their views on all, with a sense of unique insight and a belief that they know best.

The article's critical examination of the 'great man' theory and its modern manifestations in the form of anti-heroes or villains highlights the complex and problematic nature of this historical concept, which continues to shape perceptions of power and influence in the contemporary world."
